slides.title: Your app is mostly other people's code
slides.summary: A typical frontend pulls in hundreds of packages. Any one of them can be vulnerable, or turn malicious overnight.
body: Most of the code in a modern bundle, and almost all the code that runs during npm install, comes from node_modules. You chose about a dozen packages; they chose the other thousand.

ul: Vulnerable packages: honest code with a bug (a CVE). The fix is to update to a patched version.
Malicious packages: code written to attack you, published through a stolen maintainer account, a typosquat or a worm. The fix is to not install it, and to assume breach if you did.

body: <mark>Every dependency is code you ship with full access to your page and, at install time, to your laptops and CI.</mark>

body.note: Scanners built for CVEs often miss malware: a brand-new malicious version has no CVE yet. You need tools for both problems.

cells.text: event-stream: new maintainer added a wallet stealer
Log4Shell (Java): deep transitive dependency, exploited within hours
polyfill.io: domain sold, CDN served malware to 100k+ sites
axios 1.14.1 / 0.30.4: hijacked account, RAT via install script
Pin, delay, and block at the proxy

figure.alt: A dependency tree: your app depends on a few direct packages, which pull in many transitive packages. One transitive package, deep in the tree, is compromised. Two red paths lead out of it. Into the bundle: the code ships to users' browsers and can, for example, rewrite crypto wallet addresses or steal form data, as in the September 2025 chalk and debug compromise. Into install scripts: a postinstall script runs on developer laptops and CI, steals npm, GitHub and cloud tokens, and uses them to publish infected versions of more packages, which is how the Shai-Hulud worm spread to hundreds of packages in 2025.

slides.title: Why keeping dependencies up to date matters
slides.summary: Attackers now exploit flaws within days, often before a patch exists. A slow update cycle leaves you exposed for weeks.
body: When a vulnerability is published, the advisory is also a guide for attackers. The time between disclosure and exploitation has collapsed:

ul: Mandiant measured a mean time-to-exploit of 63 days in 2018–19. By 2024 it was −1 day, and for 2025 it estimates −7 days: exploitation typically starts before most teams have patched.
Automated scanners probe the whole internet for a new flaw within hours of a proof of concept appearing.
Fixes are only released for supported versions. Maintainers patch the latest line, sometimes one before it, rarely more.
Small updates are cheap. A patch bump is minutes; three skipped majors is a migration project.
You can ship an emergency fix the same day, because the path to it is already clear.
Compliance asks for it: PCI DSS requirement 6.3.3 wants critical patches installed within one month; the EU Cyber Resilience Act requires security updates for software products.
Bonus: performance improvements, bug fixes and new browser features.

body: <mark>Up to date doesn't mean installing every release the minute it's published. Update continuously, but let brand-new versions age a few days first.</mark>

figure.alt: Bar chart of mean time-to-exploit in days, as reported by Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence. 2018 to 2019: 63 days. 2020 to 2021: 44 days. 2021 to 2022: 32 days. 2023: 5 days. 2024: minus 1 day. 2025: about minus 7 days (estimate). A negative number means exploitation typically began before a patch was available. The lesson: a monthly or quarterly update cycle is far slower than attackers.

slides.title: Upgrade debt and support windows
slides.summary: Every skipped release makes the next security fix more expensive. Unsupported versions get no fixes at all.
body: Falling behind compounds. Breaking changes pile up, peer dependencies stop lining up, and the day an urgent CVE lands, you face a migration project before you can apply a one-line fix.

ul: Each major is a set of breaking changes. Skipping three means doing all of them at once, under pressure.
Peer dependencies lock together: an old framework pins old versions of its UI kit, test runner and build tools.
End of life is a hard stop. Once a version leaves its support window, new CVEs in it are never fixed.

body: <mark>Treat upgrades as routine maintenance with a schedule, not a project you start when something breaks.</mark>

body.note: Angular's ng update runs automatic migrations between majors. Use it one major at a time, and read the update guide at angular.dev/update-guide.

cells.text: Each major: 6 months active + 12 months LTS
Stay within the last two majors
No LTS: only the latest release

figure.alt: Two teams receive the same critical security fix, released only in the newest major version of a framework. Team A updates every week: it is one patch behind, so it applies the fix in a small pull request the same day. Team B updates once a year: it is three major versions behind, so to get the fix it must first work through three sets of breaking changes and peer-dependency conflicts, which takes weeks while the vulnerability stays exploitable. Old majors also leave their support window and stop getting fixes at all.

slides.title: The vocabulary of vulnerabilities
slides.summary: CVE, GHSA, CVSS, EPSS, KEV, SBOM, VEX: what each term means and what it's for.
body: Security tools and advisories use a shared vocabulary. You need it to read a scanner report or a vendor notice.
<mark>CVSS says how bad a flaw could be. EPSS and KEV say whether anyone is actually exploiting it. Prioritise with all three.</mark>

body.more: Why the NVD isn't enough on its own
body.text: The US National Vulnerability Database has had big backlogs adding details to CVEs since 2024, and NIST said in 2026 it would prioritise CVEs in CISA KEV and in software used by the federal government. For npm packages, the GitHub Advisory Database and OSV are usually faster and more precise about affected version ranges.

cells.text: A unique ID for a public vulnerability, e.g. CVE-2025-55182
GitHub Security Advisory ID; the main source for npm advisories
Open, machine-readable vulnerability database across ecosystems (osv.dev)
Severity score 0–10: how bad it could be
Probability (0–1) of exploitation in the next 30 days
Catalogue of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild
Software bill of materials: every component and version (CycloneDX, SPDX)
A statement that a product is or isn't affected by a CVE
Software composition analysis: tools that scan your dependencies
Whether your code can actually call the vulnerable function

slides.title: How dependency scanners (SCA) work
slides.summary: They read your lockfile, match every exact version against vulnerability and malware databases, add context, and propose fixes.
body: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools all follow the same pipeline. They differ in data quality, context and how well they fix things.

ul: Inventory from the lockfile, not package.json: ^1.2.0 could mean many versions; the lockfile says exactly which one is installed, including transitive packages.
Match each package@version against advisory databases (GitHub Advisory Database, OSV, NVD) and malware feeds.
Add context: is it a devDependency? Is the vulnerable function reachable? Is the deployed service internet-facing?
Fix: open an upgrade pull request, or block a build or download by policy.

body: <mark>Most vulnerable packages are transitive: you didn't install them, something you installed did.</mark>

ul: First update the direct dependency that pulls it in; that's the clean fix.
If it has no release yet, force a patched version with overrides (npm), pnpm.overrides or resolutions (Yarn), and remove the override once upstream catches up.

code: npm explain minimist            # why is this installed?
npm ls minimist --all           # every copy in the tree
// package.json: force a patched transitive version

figure.alt: Five steps from left to right. 1, Inventory: read package-lock.json or an SBOM to list every package and exact version, direct and transitive. 2, Match: compare each package and version against vulnerability databases such as the GitHub Advisory Database, OSV and NVD, and against malware feeds. 3, Context: ask whether the vulnerable code ships to users or is only a dev tool, whether the vulnerable function is reachable, and whether the workload is exposed to the internet. 4, Prioritise: rank by known exploitation (CISA KEV), exploit likelihood (EPSS) and severity (CVSS). 5, Fix: open an upgrade pull request, or block the build or download by policy.

slides.title: Prioritising: fix what matters first
slides.summary: Hundreds of findings is normal. Rank by real exploitation and reachability, and set fix deadlines by risk.
body: Teams that try to fix every finding at once burn out and start ignoring the scanner. Rank instead:

ul: Does it ship or run with secrets? A bug in a build-time CLI that never sees untrusted input is low risk; the same bug in your SSR server is not.
Is it reachable? Snyk, Socket, Endor Labs and JFrog's contextual analysis check whether your code can actually hit the vulnerable path.
Is it exploited? Anything in CISA KEV jumps the queue. A high EPSS score means exploitation is likely soon.
Is a fix available? If not, mitigate (WAF rule, disable the feature) and watch for a release.

body: <mark>A KEV-listed, reachable vulnerability in an internet-facing service is an emergency, whatever its CVSS score.</mark>

body.note: Record decisions. When you accept a finding (not reachable, dev-only), write down why and set an expiry date, so it gets reviewed again.

cells.text: In CISA KEV, used by your SSR server

viz.html: Example deadlines; set your own with your security team.

figure.alt: An illustrative funnel for one frontend repo. 900 raw findings from the scanner. Remove dev-only packages that never ship to users or run with secrets: 260 remain. Keep only those where the vulnerable function is reachable from your code: 45 remain. Keep those with a fix available and real exploit risk, meaning listed in CISA KEV or with a high EPSS score, or critical and internet-exposed: 4 remain, to fix today. The rest go into the normal update flow. The numbers are illustrative.

slides.title: JFrog: Artifactory, Curation and Xray
slides.summary: JFrog puts a controlled registry between npm and your code: block bad packages before download, and scan everything you build and ship.
body: JFrog is a software supply-chain platform used by many large companies. For a frontend team it does three jobs:

ul: Artifactory is a private registry and proxy. A remote repository caches npmjs.org; a virtual repository combines it with your private packages. Every laptop and CI runner installs through it, so there's one place to control and audit.

Curation is the gate in front of the cache. Policies block package versions before they're downloaded: known malicious, critical CVEs, banned licences, or too new. JFrog is moving Xray's older “block download” feature into Curation during 2026.

Xray scans what's already inside: cached packages, builds, Docker images and release bundles. Watches choose what to scan, policies decide what's a violation (CVE severity, licence, malware), and violations can fail a build or block a release.
Contextual analysis: checks whether a CVE actually applies to your code and configuration, to cut false positives.
Secrets, IaC and SAST scanning in the same pipeline.
Frogbot: a Git bot that scans pull requests, comments on new vulnerable dependencies and opens fix PRs.
JFrog CLI: jf audit scans a project locally or in CI.

body: <mark>Because Curation blocks a bad version before it reaches a machine, its install script never runs. Scanning after install can't do that.</mark>

body.note: When a malicious version is published, the registry proxy is also your fastest kill switch: block it once, and every team is protected. Remember to purge it from the cache too.

code: jf audit --fail=true            # scan dependencies, fail on policy

figure.alt: Left to right. A developer or CI runs npm install, with .npmrc pointing at the company Artifactory instead of the public npm registry. Artifactory has a remote repository that proxies and caches npmjs.org. Before a new package version is downloaded into the cache, JFrog Curation checks it against policies: known malicious, critical CVE, banned license, or too new; a blocked package never reaches the developer. JFrog Xray continuously scans what is in Artifactory and every build and release bundle, using watches and policies, and with Advanced Security checks whether a CVE is actually applicable (contextual analysis), and scans for secrets. Frogbot comments on pull requests and opens fix PRs. Builds that violate policy can be failed.

slides.title: Wiz: from vulnerable code to real cloud risk
slides.summary: Wiz scans code, images and running cloud workloads, then ranks a CVE by whether it's deployed, exposed and near sensitive data.
body: Wiz is a cloud security platform (a CNAPP). Google completed its acquisition of Wiz in March 2026; Wiz still works across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and other clouds.

ul: Wiz Code scans repositories, pull requests and IDEs for vulnerable dependencies, secrets, infrastructure-as-code misconfigurations and code flaws, and traces each finding to where it runs in the cloud.
Wiz Cloud scans cloud accounts agentlessly, reading disks and images of VMs, containers and serverless functions to find vulnerable packages actually running in production.
Wiz Defend adds runtime threat detection and response.

The Security Graph links code, images, workloads, network exposure, identities and data. It flags toxic combinations: a vulnerable package in a service that's internet-facing and can read sensitive data.

body: <mark>The same CVE can be an emergency in one service and harmless in another. Wiz-style context tells you which is which.</mark>

body.h: Why a frontend team should care

ul: SSR and BFF servers are Node containers in the cloud, often internet-facing.
Static sites live in storage buckets and CDNs that can be misconfigured.
API keys leak into repos and front-end bundles.
During an incident, Wiz's inventory answers “where is axios 1.14.1 running right now?” across every account.

body.text: Palo Alto Networks Prisma Cloud, Orca Security, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Aqua Security and Sysdig cover similar ground. Pick based on your clouds, existing vendors and how well findings route to the right owners.

figure.alt: A graph from left to right. In code: a repository with a vulnerable package in package-lock.json, found by Wiz Code scanning the repo and pull requests, along with secrets and infrastructure-as-code misconfigurations. It builds into a container image, scanned in CI and the registry. The image runs as an SSR Node service in Kubernetes, which Wiz Cloud scans agentlessly. That service is exposed to the internet and its role can read a storage bucket with customer data. Wiz's security graph links these facts and flags the toxic combination: vulnerable, exposed, and with access to sensitive data, which should be fixed first. The same CVE in an internal batch job with no data access ranks much lower. Google completed its acquisition of Wiz in March 2026; Wiz still supports all major clouds.

slides.title: The tool landscape
slides.summary: No single tool covers everything. Combine an update bot, a CVE scanner, malware detection and a registry gate.
body: Tools fall into a few categories. Most teams combine one from each of the first three, and larger organisations add the rest.

ul: Update bots keep you current with small, frequent pull requests.
CVE scanners (SCA) find known vulnerabilities in what you've installed.
Malware detection spots packages behaving badly (install scripts, network calls, obfuscated code) before they have a CVE.
Registry gates stop bad versions entering your organisation at all.
Cloud and runtime tools show what's actually deployed and exposed.
Provenance and posture tools verify who built a package and how healthy the project is.

body: <mark>Free tools (Dependabot or Renovate, npm audit or OSV-Scanner, provenance checks) already cover the basics. Paid tools add context, malware detection and organisation-wide control.</mark>

cells.text: npm audit, OSV-Scanner, Dependabot alerts, Snyk, Mend, Sonatype, Endor Labs, JFrog Xray, Wiz Code
Socket, Snyk, Sonatype, JFrog Curation, Aikido
JFrog Artifactory + Curation, Sonatype Nexus Firewall, Cloudsmith
Wiz, Prisma Cloud, Orca, Defender for Cloud

viz.html: Examples, not endorsements. Features change quickly; check each vendor's current docs.

slides.title: A practical update workflow
slides.summary: Automate small weekly updates with tests, delay brand-new versions, and fast-track security fixes.
body: A workflow that keeps a large frontend current without drowning the team:

ul: Weekly, grouped PRs: one PR for Angular packages, one for testing tools, and so on, so related packages move together.
Automerge the safe ones: patch updates of devDependencies when CI is green.
A release-age delay of a few days (Renovate's minimumReleaseAge, Dependabot's cooldown) lets the community catch malicious versions first.
Security fixes skip the queue: vulnerability PRs open immediately and are labelled for fast review.
Majors get a ticket: plan them within the support window, one major at a time.
Good tests make all of this safe. Without them, every update is a gamble.

body: <mark>The goal is boring updates: small, frequent, tested and mostly automatic.</mark>

slides.title: Hardening installs and publishing
slides.summary: Lock versions, don't run install scripts you don't need, and publish with trusted publishing and provenance.

ul: Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci, so CI uses exactly the reviewed versions.
Don't run install scripts you don't need. pnpm 10+ skips dependency lifecycle scripts unless you allow them (onlyBuiltDependencies); with npm, use --ignore-scripts where you can.
Give CI the least access: short-lived credentials, no production secrets in jobs that install packages.
Review new dependencies before adding them: maintainers, activity, download trend, install scripts, size, and OpenSSF Scorecard.
Use trusted publishing (OIDC from CI) instead of long-lived npm tokens, plus phishing-resistant 2FA. npm moved publishing in this direction after the 2025 attacks.
Publish with provenance, so users can check which repo and workflow built the package (npm audit signatures).

body: <mark>Most 2025–26 npm attacks ran through install scripts and stolen long-lived tokens. Removing both closes the main path.</mark>
code: npm ci --ignore-scripts      # exact lockfile, no install scripts
npm audit --omit=dev         # what ships to users
npm audit signatures         # verify registry signatures + provenance
minimumReleaseAge: 4320      # minutes: skip versions < 3 days old

slides.title: Scanning your own code and the running app
slides.summary: Dependency scans cover other people's code. SAST checks yours, DAST attacks the running app, and penetration testers find what tools miss.
body: A complete programme scans at several layers:

ul: SAST (static analysis) reads your source for dangerous patterns: user input reaching innerHTML, eval or a SQL query. Examples: GitHub CodeQL, Semgrep, SonarQube.
DAST (dynamic testing) attacks a running build like an outsider: it crawls pages, fuzzes inputs and checks headers and cookies. Examples: ZAP (formerly OWASP ZAP), Burp Suite, HCL AppScan.
Penetration testing is skilled people chaining issues together, such as business-logic flaws, IDOR and auth bypasses, that scanners rarely find.
Bug bounties pay outside researchers to keep looking after launch.
Run SAST on every pull request and block new high-severity findings.
Run a ZAP baseline scan against the staging deployment nightly.
npm audit already runs on every npm install (the audit setting is on by default); make CI fail on it with npm audit --audit-level=high --omit=dev.

body: <mark>Tools find the common bugs cheaply. People find the clever ones. You need both.</mark>

slides.title: SBOMs and incident response
slides.summary: When a package is compromised, the first question is “are we affected?”. An SBOM answers it in minutes.
body: A software bill of materials (SBOM) lists every component and version in a build, in a standard format (CycloneDX or SPDX). Generate one per release and store it with the artifact.

ul: Answer “are we affected?” fast: search SBOMs and lockfiles across every repo and image.
Customers and regulators ask for them: US federal software suppliers, and the EU Cyber Resilience Act's documentation requirements.
Feed them to tools: Dependency-Track, JFrog Xray and Wiz can watch SBOMs and alert when a new CVE matches.

body.h: If you installed a malicious version

ul: Assume the machine or CI runner is compromised: the install script ran with its permissions.
Rotate every credential it could reach: npm, GitHub, cloud, API keys.
Rebuild runners, check what was published or deployed from them, then pin a known-good version and block the bad one at your registry proxy.

body: <mark>Removing the bad package isn't enough. Its install script already ran; rotate the secrets it could see.</mark>
code: npm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx > sbom.json   # from the lockfile
syft my-image:1.4.2 -o cyclonedx-json          # from a container image

figure.alt: A timeline of responding to a malicious release such as axios 1.14.1 in March 2026. Minute 0: an advisory or a tool alert names the bad versions. Minutes 5 to 15: query SBOMs and lockfiles across all repos and images to find which ones resolved the bad version during the exposure window. Minutes 15 to 30: block the versions in the registry proxy, pin the last good version, and purge caches. Minutes 30 to 60: on any machine or CI runner that installed it, assume compromise: rotate npm, GitHub, cloud and API tokens, rebuild runners, and review what was published or deployed. Afterwards: write up what happened and tighten policy, for example a minimum release age.
